For decades, Nollywood actor Emeka Ike has been one of the faces associated with the industry’s romantic leading men. From his piercing gaze and charming screen presence to the effortless affection he brings to romantic roles, Ike built a reputation as one of Nollywood’s quintessential lover boys, particularly during the home-video era of the 1990s and early 2000s.
Now 59, the veteran actor appears unwilling to relinquish that familiar screen identity. Rather than allow age to distance him from the romantic roles that endeared him to audiences, Ike seems to have embraced a more mature version of the character, demonstrating that the appeal of a screen lover boy is not necessarily diminished by time.
His latest outing in Mother’s Bargain, a Nollywood drama released on Uchenna Mbunabo TV, has once again drawn attention to that enduring appeal. Playing Chief Coker, a wealthy politician whose affection and emotional maturity gradually transform an initially transactional marriage into a genuine love story, Ike revisits a character type that helped define his career, this time with the composure and tenderness of a more seasoned performer.
Mother’s Bargain, directed by Ben Cassie and written by Chioma Akpan, centred on Adaora (Chinenye Nnebe), a young woman caught between her mother’s ambitions and her desire to determine her own future. Her mother, Felicia (Charity Onah), whose life had been shaped by poverty, hardship, and abandonment, saw marriage to wealthy politician Chief Coker (Emeka Ike) as the family’s best chance to escape financial difficulties.
Adaora, however, was already in a relationship with Chike, whose marriage proposal was thrown into uncertainty following his arrest for wire fraud. Under sustained pressure from Felicia, she eventually agreed to marry Chief Coker, although the union began more as an arrangement of convenience than a genuine expression of love.
But the marriage took an unexpected turn when Chief Coker demonstrated a tenderness that contradicted the conventional portrayal of wealthy older men in Nollywood romance dramas.
Following a hypertension crisis linked to tampered medication and Felicia’s subsequent death from a stroke, Adaora was left to confront the consequences of the arrangement. She eventually confessed her mother’s original intentions to her husband.

Rather than retaliate, Chief Coker granted her a divorce, provided financial support, and helped secure her a job. Only after experiencing life away from him did Adaora recognise the depth of her feelings and return to rebuild their relationship.
The film ended with the couple reconciled and looking towards a future together, leaving viewers with the impression that their complicated journey had finally found its happy ending.
Its appeal was reflected in its impressive performance on YouTube, where it eventually garnered over 12 million views. Much of the audience’s affection for the film rested on Emeka Ike’s portrayal of Chief Coker, whose quiet confidence, generosity, and emotional maturity earned him admiration as Nollywood’s latest “OG lover boy”.
For many viewers, there was little reason to expect another chapter. But Mother’s Bargain 2, released on November 2, 2026, returns to the couple’s lives, demonstrating that reconciliation does not necessarily guarantee a trouble-free marriage.
Directed again by Ben Cassie, the sequel retains the central characters but introduces new complications that threaten the domestic peace established in the first instalment.
This time, Adaora and Chief Coker must confront infertility, unsuccessful in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) attempts and the unexpected arrival of a son from the politician’s past.
The young man, Ade (Kelvin Utulu), is 26 years old and previously unknown to Chief Coker. His mother, Alicia, also returns to the politician’s life, bringing with her tensions that threaten to unsettle his marriage.
A DNA test confirming paternity at 99.9 per cent establishes Ade’s place in the family. However, the revelation does little to guarantee harmony. Instead, it raises questions about inheritance, family loyalty, acceptance, and Adaora’s place in a household that suddenly has a new heir.
The situation becomes even more complicated as Alicia’s presence and influence begin to affect the newly reunited couple. With Adaora already struggling with the emotional burden of infertility, the arrival of Chief Coker’s adult son creates another test for a marriage that viewers had assumed was finally secure. Would love prevail again?
If there is one reason Mother’s Bargain 2 sustains the appeal of its predecessor, it is Emeka Ike’s return as Chief Coker.
Mr Ike doesn’t try to reinvent the character. Instead, he builds on the qualities that made the character memorable in the first film. His portrayal blends authority with gentleness, giving the character a reassuring presence without making him seem overly sentimental.
The description of Chief Coker as an “OG lover boy” is particularly fitting. He represents a kind of romantic masculinity that is increasingly appealing within the film’s narrative: a man who can exercise authority without intimidation and demonstrate affection without making a spectacle of it.
In the sequel, Chief Coker faces the difficult task of processing the discovery of a son he never knew existed, managing Alicia’s return and protecting his marriage from the tensions surrounding his expanded family.
He handles these developments with the composure expected of a veteran actor. Rather than relying on exaggerated expressions or explosive confrontations, the veteran allows disappointment, suspicion, and emotional pain to emerge through measured dialogue and restrained performances.
His strongest moments come when Chief Coker discovers further betrayals, including attempts to undermine Adaora. The actor gives these scenes the necessary emotional weight without allowing the character to lose the dignity that defines him.
This consistency makes his performance particularly effective. Chief Coker is not an entirely new character in Part 2; he is the same man whose kindness helped transform an initially transactional marriage into a genuine relationship.
Despite its engaging performances, Mother’s Bargain 2 does not quite possess the thematic freshness of the original.
The first film drew much of its strength from the unusual circumstances surrounding Adaora’s marriage. It explored poverty, maternal desperation, financial insecurity, and the difficult choices women sometimes face when their futures are determined by family expectations.
Its most compelling achievement was the gradual transformation of a marriage founded on deception into a relationship built on genuine affection. Chief Coker’s unexpected decency also challenged the familiar Nollywood stereotype of the wealthy older man who uses money to manipulate younger women.
The sequel, however, relies more heavily on familiar family-drama devices: a long-lost child, a returning former partner, inheritance concerns, maternal interference, and marital insecurity.
These developments are not inherently uninteresting. Indeed, they provide sufficient conflict to sustain the narrative and give the returning characters new challenges. However, they make the film feel more conventional than its predecessor.
The infertility storyline, in particular, could have been explored more deeply. It offers an opportunity to explore the emotional and social pressures of childlessness, especially in marriages where family expectations and questions of inheritance become intertwined.
Instead, much of the attention shifts towards the intrigues surrounding Ade’s arrival and Alicia’s influence.
However, Mother’s Bargain 2 may not reinvent the original, but it offers a reasonable continuation of a story that resonated with a large YouTube audience.
Where the first film explored whether genuine affection could emerge from a marriage founded on financial desperation, the sequel examines whether that affection can survive the complications of a partner’s past, infertility, and the arrival of a previously unknown child.
The film works best when it lets Mr Ike and Ms Nnebe carry the story’s emotional weight. Their chemistry remains its strongest asset, while Mr Ike’s restrained portrayal of Chief Coker provides the consistency needed to hold the narrative together.
Some of the new conflicts feel predictable, and the sequel occasionally sacrifices thematic depth for familiar family intrigues. Still, its emotional continuity and returning performances give viewers plenty of reason to stay invested.
For audiences who thought Adaora and Chief Coker’s story had ended with the first film, the sequel offers a reminder that even the most unlikely love stories have their unfinished chapters.
Mother’s Bargain 2 is streaming on Uchenna Mbunabo TV on YouTube
